compatibility.title: Which MG Models Use the 15E4E?
compatibility.intro: The 15E4E is SAIC's 1.5‑litre turbocharged GDI petrol engine, part of the SGE (Small Gasoline Engine) family developed in partnership with GM. It was introduced around 2016 and powers MG's larger models, including the HS SUV and the earlier GS crossover.

costGuide.labourLine: Fitting a 15E4E typically takes 8-11 hours at £65-£85/hr (independent) - confirm exact labour when comparing quotes. [PATTERN DATA - based on typical transverse 4‑cylinder turbo petrol labour]

What genuinely moves the 15E4E replacement price is the engine's configuration - petrol-only and PHEV (hybrid) versions differ significantly in ancillary components and wiring. failures.title: MG 15E4E Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Carbon buildup on intake valves (GDI) - 40k-80k miles
items.onset: 40,000-80,000 miles [PATTERN DATA - characteristic of direct‑injection petrol engines]
items.whatHappens: Like all direct‑injection petrol engines, the 15E4E's intake valves are not washed by fuel, allowing oil vapour and crankcase gases to bake onto valve stems and backs. This restricts airflow, causing rough idle, hesitation, misfires, and reduced performance. Carbon buildup is one of the most frequently reported issues with the 15E4E.
items.repairVsReplace: Walnut‑blast cleaning of the intake valves typically costs £300-£600 and restores performance. If ignored, severe carbon can cause drivability issues but rarely writes off the engine. This is a repair, not a replacement trigger.

items.title: Crankcase blow-by and pressure issues - 60k+ miles
items.onset: 60,000+ miles [PATTERN DATA - reported on some SAIC turbo engines]
items.whatHappens: Some 15E4E engines have been reported to suffer from crankcase pressure buildup caused by combustion gases passing the piston rings and entering the crankcase. In severe cases, this can force oil out of the dipstick tube or cause oil contamination. This issue appears to be more common on engines that have been driven hard or have had extended oil service intervals.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, piston ring replacement and crankcase ventilation system overhaul may be sufficient - budget £800-£1,500. If ignored, the engine can suffer from oil starvation and bearing damage, which typically writes off the engine.

items.title: Timing chain stretch - 80k-120k miles (higher-mileage units)
items.onset: 80,000-120,000 miles [PATTERN DATA - common on chain‑driven turbo petrol engines]
items.whatHappens: The 15E4E uses a chain‑driven timing system. On higher‑mileage units, the timing chain can stretch, leading to timing inaccuracy, rough running, and in severe cases, chain failure with catastrophic engine damage. This is less common than on some other SAIC engines but is reported on higher‑mileage examples.
items.repairVsReplace: Chain and tensioner replacement costs £500-£1,000 if caught early (rattle on cold start). If the chain breaks, the engine is almost certainly scrap - full replacement is the only viable option.

failures.goodYearsLine: Later 15E4E units (2019 onwards) received revised piston ring and crankcase ventilation designs; blow-by reports are less frequent on these newer revisions, though carbon buildup remains characteristic of all GDI engines.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the 15E4E
variants.intro: The 15E4E is part of SAIC's SGE family of 1.5‑litre turbo engines. It appears in two very different configurations: petrol-only and PHEV (plug‑in hybrid). These are not interchangeable. Where to find the code: The engine code is stamped on the engine block, typically on the front face near the timing cover or on the driver's side. It also appears on the V5C registration document under “Engine number”. A VIN decoder will confirm the exact factory build code. Which codes get confused with it: The 15E4E is frequently confused with the naturally aspirated 15S4C (1.5‑litre, no turbo) - they are completely different engines. It is also related to the GM LFV engine family but has different calibration and ancillaries. The 15E4E should not be confused with the 15E4F (later revision) if one exists. Why fitting the wrong revision matters: A PHEV‑spec 15E4E has different wiring, sensors, and ECU calibration compared to a petrol‑only unit. Fitting the wrong version will cause compatibility issues, potentially requiring a full ECU and loom swap. Always confirm whether your car is the standard 1.5T or the EHS Hybrid before ordering a replacement.

relatives.description: The plug-in hybrid version of the same engine, used in the MG HS EHS (PHEV) and Roewe eRX5. It has the same basic architecture but different ancillaries, wiring, and ECU calibration. Not a straight swap with petrol-only units.

A later revision of the 1.5-litre turbo, introduced around 2020 with revised emissions calibration and updated injector part numbers. If you're buying a post-2020 MG, this may be the code you'll find.

The naturally aspirated 1.5-litre 4-cylinder that shares the MG HS nameplate but is a completely different engine design (MPI vs GDI). Replacement buyers should ensure they are sourcing the correct code - the 15E4E and 15S4C are not interchangeable, and fitting the wrong one will cause ECU mismatches.
derived) - Early SAIC 1.5-litre turbo engines (pre-2016) were based more directly on GM's LFV family. The 15E4E represents a significant upgrade with improved injection and calibration.

The 15E4E shares its basic architecture with GM's 1.5-litre turbo used in the Opel Astra and Zafira, among others. However, calibration, ancillaries, and mounting points differ - do not assume interchangeability without checking part numbers.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement 15E4E - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used 15E4E makes sense for lower‑value MG GS models (sub‑£5,000) where a recon investment doesn't stack up. The key risks are carbon buildup, injector health, and timing chain condition - a used unit without a documented carbon‑clean, injector replacement, or chain history is a gamble. Only buy with compression test results and, if possible, a bore‑scope inspection of the intake valves. PHEV and petrol‑only units are not interchangeable.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: The recommended route for most 15E4E replacements, especially for MG HS owners. A proper recon includes a full carbon‑clean of the intake valves, new injectors, new timing chain and tensioner, and a rebuilt turbocharger. For a £1,800-£3,500 investment, you get a 12-24 month warranty and an engine that should be good for another 80k+ miles. This is the sensible choice for HS owners in the £8,000-£18,000 bracket.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full 15E4E rebuild is generally only justified for numbers‑matching cars or where the block itself is in pristine condition. Typical costs £3,000-£4,800. For most owners, reconditioned is the smarter and more cost‑effective choice.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: All our vetted specialists offer supply‑only, supply‑and‑fit, or full workshop installation. Fitting through the network includes a 12‑month warranty on parts and labour, with nationwide delivery to your chosen garage or home address.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The 15E4E is found across MG models with varying values. For an MG GS worth £3,000-£8,000, a £1,800+ recon may be borderline - consider a used unit or evaluate scrap value first. For MG HS hosts in the £8,000-£18,000 bracket, a reconditioned 15E4E is financially viable and often the most sensible decision. Always compare the lowest viable replacement cost against your car's current market value - if the engine repair exceeds 60% of the vehicle's worth, scrapping may be the better outcome.

items.question: How much does an MG 15E4E engine replacement cost?
items.answer: A reconditioned 15E4E typically costs £1,800-£3,500 supply-only, with fitted prices ranging from £2,190-£4,100 depending on labour and warranty. Used units are cheaper at £800-£1,800 supply-only but carry higher risk of carbon buildup and injector health. A full rebuild can exceed £4,800 if the block requires machining. PHEV and petrol-only versions differ significantly in ancillaries and wiring - pricing varies accordingly.

items.question: What is the most common failure on the 15E4E?
items.answer: The most widely reported issue is carbon buildup on the intake valves, a characteristic of direct-injection (GDI) engines, which can cause rough idle, hesitation, and misfires. Walnut-blast cleaning typically costs £300-£600 and restores performance. Crankcase blow-by and timing chain stretch are also reported on higher-mileage units. Regular use of quality fuel and occasional Italian tune-ups can reduce carbon formation.

items.question: Which MG models use the 15E4E engine?
items.answer: The 15E4E is fitted to the MG GS (2016-2019), MG HS (2018-present) and the MG HS EHS (PHEV variant). It is also used in selected MG ZS models in some markets, but UK-market ZS typically uses the 15S4C or 10E4E. It is not used in the MG3, which uses the 15S4C (1.5 NA) or 10E4E (1.0T).

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned 15E4E?
items.answer: For most owners, a reconditioned 15E4E is the better choice because it includes a carbon-clean, new injectors, new timing chain, and a rebuilt turbo. Used units are only advisable for very low-value cars (sub-£5,000) where the cost of a recon cannot be justified. Always request compression test results and, if possible, a bore-scope inspection of the intake valves. PHEV and petrol-only units are not interchangeable - confirm the exact specification before buying.

items.question: How do I know if my MG has the 15E4E and not the 15S4C or 10E4E?
items.answer: The engine code is stamped on the front or side of the block and on the V5C registration document under "Engine number". The 15E4E is a 1.5-litre turbo - the 15S4C is naturally aspirated (no turbo). The 10E4E is a 1.0-litre three-cylinder - visually different and different engine number prefix. The PHEV version of the 15E4E has additional hybrid ancillaries - the engine code prefix alone won't tell you this; check the vehicle specification.

items.question: Is the 15E4E a reliable engine overall?
items.answer: Yes, when properly maintained. The carbon buildup is a maintenance issue rather than a fundamental design flaw, and the engine is generally durable with good parts availability. Regular oil changes every 10,000 miles or annually are essential. Use premium fuel to keep injectors clean and reduce carbon formation. Later revisions (2019 onwards) addressed crankcase blow-by and piston ring concerns.
